1f9k2i7:247: The section "Review Agent Also Learns the Wrong Way" reveals three major traps in self-learning systems, each pointing to a fundamental problem: learning is not the same as recording everything. The essence of over-abstraction is that execution context is lost during information distillation; the root of log-style records is treating logs as memory; the essence of anthropomorphic errors is inferring long-term preferences from a single behavioral mistake. Notably, each type of failure has a corresponding engineering constraint: "steps must be reproducible" prevents over-abstraction, the "two-strike rule" prevents anthropomorphic preferences, and "one-time events are not written to memory" prevents log-style records. These constraints look simple, but they are engineering wisdom accumulated from hitting pitfalls, not something that could be fully specified at the initial design stage.

1jtlv76:280: The design of Review Agent is essentially about completely decoupling the roles of "executor" and "evaluator." This decoupling is not intuitive in engineering, because having the same model both do the work and evaluate it seems more resource-efficient. But winty points out a counter-intuitive fact in the article: during self-evaluation, the "sunk cost" of execution suppresses the objectivity of evaluation—an Agent finds it hard to give negative feedback on its own work, because that conflicts with the execution mindset of "I just tried my best." This psychological mechanism holds true for both humans and models, which is why Hermes chose physical isolation: one Agent runs the task, another Agent reviews it. The data showing that independent review achieves roughly 3x higher hit rates on subsequent tasks compared to self-reflection strongly validates the necessity of this design.

4ash4h:219: The design of prioritizing Patch over new entries solves the maintenance problem of multi-version conflicts. If every review created a new entry instead of merging updates, the same fact would be recorded multiple times, versions would contradict each other, and ultimately retrieval quality would degrade. The Patch mechanism ensures that core entries converge to a stable state over time, with incremental supplementation as the main evolution path rather than infinite new additions—providing a sustainable path for long-term maintenance. .hermes/review-feedback.md, as the entry point for human feedback, integrates human oversight into the automated process, keeping the evolution direction of the Review Agent always under control.
69miw:272: If the Nudge Engine is Hermes's "switch," then the Review Agent is its "mind." The design I admire most when reading the Hermes source code is this part. It doesn't let the "agent executing the task" review itself; instead, it runs a separate agent dedicated to reflection, working quietly in the background. This seems like a small thing, but it solves a very fundamental engineering problem: having someone who is currently doing the work judge whether they just did a good job always ends up verbose, self-congratulatory, and useless. The Review Agent solves exactly this problem. It changes its role, changes its prompt, changes its set of judgment criteria, and focuses solely on "reviewing + deciding what to remember."
